newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Airlines eyes strategic partner.
newsitem.headline: China Airlines eyes strategic partner.

text.p: Taiwan carrier China Airlines was aiming to facilitate its globalisation plan through the sale of a 16 percent existing stake by its majority shareholder to a strategic partner, chairman Chiang Hung-i said on Monday.
But Chiang declined to comment on talk that British Airways was likely to buy the stake from the China Aviation Development Foundation, which holds 82 percent of the airline.

"I can't say that British Airways is not a good strategic partner," Chiang told reporters in Hong Kong. "However, it's in our planning stage and (we are) not ready yet to unveil which carrier could be a stratgeic partner in our globalisation."
"We haven't talked to any carrier as yet in real terms," he added. "There are a few carriers in our minds in priority."

China Airlines said in May last year that the Foundation planned to release a 16 percent stake in the carrier to diversify its shareholding structure. The plan was postponed to the first half of 1997 due to delays in government approval.

Chiang said the key factor in choosing potential institutional investors or a strategic partner was that the partner should not be taking a stake in China Airlines as a short-term investment for financial gain.

"Also they must recognise...the synergy of being together with China Airlines for the future business development and must be in a very cooporative position working together with us for the future aviation development and must be aiming for the long-term," the chairman said.
"All those factors will have to be included in our dialogues before we make a final decision," Chiang said.
The Foundation is seeking to place 210 million shares or 16 percent of the Taiwan carrier.
"That's part of the original plan that eventually the Foundation's shareholding in China Airlines will progressively be reduced further," Chiang said.
He said there was no set plan on how many shares the Foundation would retain in China Airlines, and added that the airline hoped the dilution process would meet its strategic partnerships planning.

"But as you know that once the shares are released, we are giving more opportunity and more shares be traded in the open market and that's part of the plan in fact that we will (reach) our goal to be privatised as a truely public company," he said.
